summary:
When NASA replaced the 1km MODIS sensor with the 375m VIIRS sensor in 2012, it introduced a major discontinuity in satellite fire records. Because VIIRS detects smaller and cooler burns, raw historical data can't be directly compared to modern fire seasons.

I built FireLookout to standardize this record and map active fires to downwind health risks.

Using biome-specific calibration ratios, FireLookout normalizes 24 years of NASA FIRMS data (2001–2024) into a continuous burning calendar so analysts can isolate true seasonal anomalies from sensor bias.

What sets the tool apart is its downwind exposure engine: it pairs active FIRMS fire radiative power with live wind vectors to project smoke plumes, then intersects those plumes with NASA SEDAC gridded population data (GPWv4) to estimate exposure among seniors (65+), young children, and outdoor agricultural workers.
details:
How it works

FireLookout combines a 24-year historical climate archive with a real-time smoke exposure monitor:

  • Sensor Harmonization: Converts fragmented observations from NASA’s legacy MODIS (1,000m) and modern VIIRS (375m) sensors into consistent Harmonized Hotspot Units (HHU). By applying peer-reviewed, biome-specific calibration factors (K = 3.90 - 4.40), it makes 2001–2024 fire records directly comparable.
  • Burning Activity Calendar: Plots 24 years of calibrated fire data across key regions (Pantanal, Southeast Australia, Congo Basin, California) in a 2D matrix, benchmarking each month against its historical median to isolate true anomalies from sensor bias.
  • Real-Time Smoke & Exposure Modeling: Pulls active fire radiative power (FRP) from the NASA FIRMS API and combines it with live 10m wind forecasts from Open-Meteo (NOAA GFS / ECMWF) to project downwind smoke cones. Intersecting those cones with NASA SEDAC population data (GPWv4) calculates immediate exposure for communities in the plume's path.


Why it matters

  • Unbiased Historical Comparison: Land managers and climate scientists can tell whether a fire season is genuinely anomalous rather than mistaking VIIRS’s higher sensor sensitivity for a sudden surge in real-world burning.
  • Actionable Community Triage: Instead of just plotting red dots on a map, FireLookout shows who is actually breathing the smoke downwind, breaking down exposure estimates for vulnerable groups, including seniors (65+), children under 5, and outdoor agricultural workers.


Intended impact

FireLookout is designed to turn satellite fire data from passive retrospective reporting into active public health protection. By combining long-term seasonal baselines with live downwind smoke modeling, emergency managers, local health authorities, and agricultural coordinators can:

  • Anticipate high-risk burn windows weeks in advance using calibrated historical baselines.
  • Protect vulnerable communities early by distributing N95 masks and respiratory guidance before heavy smoke arrives.
  • Allocate firefighting resources more effectively based on real-time fire intensity and downwind population exposure.


Tech stack & data sources

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS v4.
    • NASA Earthdata FIRMS REST API: MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS (S-NPP / NOAA-20) near real-time detections and historical archives.
    • NASA SEDAC GPWv4: Gridded Population of the World demographic data.
    • Open-Meteo API: Live 10m surface wind vectors from NOAA GFS and ECMWF models.
  • Deployment: Vercel edge network configured with custom build caching and vendor code-splitting.


What makes it creative

Most wildfire tools treat detections in isolation as static pins on a map. Instead of building another point-plotter, FireLookout connects three distinct scientific layers inside a single lightweight web app:

  • Instrument Calibration: Resolving the spatial resolution mismatch between legacy MODIS and modern VIIRS sensors so 24 years of fire data can be read on one continuous scale.
  • Atmospheric Physics: Translating live surface wind vectors into real-time downwind smoke dispersion cones rather than looking only at the burn perimeter.
  • Demographic Intersection: Overlaying those smoke corridors onto gridded population data so responders can see the human health risk of a fire while it is still actively burning.


Key engineering & design trade-offs

  • Data Accuracy vs. API Rate Limits: NASA’s FIRMS API caps historical area queries at 5-day windows and lacks a monthly aggregation endpoint. To build a 24-year calendar without hitting rate limits or overloading the browser, I wrote a pre-compilation pipeline that samples representative mid-month windows across all 288 months for each biome.
  • Regional Biome Differences: Fire behavior varies wildly across ecosystems, so applying a single global calibration factor would distort the data. Instead, I implemented biome-specific multipliers tailored to tropical wetlands, temperate eucalyptus forests, sub-Saharan agricultural zones, and Mediterranean chaparral.
  • Field-Ready Performance: Emergency coordinators often work on laptops with spotty connections. I kept the interface lightweight with high-contrast visuals, minimal dependencies, and bundled offline fallback datasets so the app stays responsive even under poor network conditions.
